There is genuine disagreement among sources about whether watering plants during the day — particularly at midday — is harmful or simply suboptimal. The majority of sources, including the RHS [d8] and a University of Georgia extension source [d14], advise against watering in the heat of the day, primarily because much water is lost to evaporation and because moisture left on leaves overnight (from afternoon watering) can promote fungal disease. [d2] and [d4] both recommend early morning as the most efficient time, with [d4] explicitly stating to "avoid the middle of the day to avoid water loss to evaporation." [d5], citing a plant biochemist, similarly states that "water will evaporate before it can properly wet the soil" when watering in full sun, and [d10] warns that "watering during the day can increase risk of disease." [d11] acknowledges that "conflicting advice" exists but concludes that morning watering is best in hot weather. However, [d7] directly challenges this consensus, stating that "the oft-repeated belief that watering on a hot sunny day will damage your plants is a gardening myth that's been debunked by science," and that midday watering is "perfectly okay" though not the most efficient. [d9] similarly calls leaf burn from midday watering "a common garden myth in most instances," supported by researchers. Notably, [d12] takes yet another angle, stating that "99% of your plants, indoors and out should only be watered during the day" — meaning not at night — recommending early morning or early evening for best absorption.
